title: Planning an open house
body: Ten students of Class 12 were picked at random and asked to plan their school's open house, with full autonomy. At the first meeting the members were excited but also unsure: they did not know one another well, were unclear about what exactly the open house should include, and wondered whether they would fit in. In the next two meetings there were heated arguments about who would lead the committee, who would control the small budget and who would do which task. Gradually things settled down. The members agreed on rules such as meeting every Monday, deciding by vote and finishing assigned work on time, and they began to speak of the committee as 'we'. They then divided the work, prepared the displays and ran the open house successfully. A week after the event, the committee was dissolved.

title: The cleanliness drive
body: A school organised a one-day cleanliness drive. Class 12A worked as a single large group of 30 students. Only the total area cleaned by the whole class was announced at the end, nobody recorded who had cleaned what, and the result was not compared with that of any other class. Many students in 12A later admitted that they had spent much of the time chatting. Class 12B was divided into five teams of six. Each student's assigned patch was recorded, the principal told them that the drive was vital for the school's hygiene ranking, and every team's result was displayed on the notice board alongside the results of other classes. Class 12B cleaned a much larger area per student than Class 12A.
